We're living longer and longer lives, however, we haven't made a massive dent in extending youth. All of the extensions we are seeing in average life expectancy (that really took off in the 20th century) are occurring by extending the elderly years, as opposed to dilating the period that we are young, exuberant, and physically able (this doesn't even begin to consider our psychological interpretations and discrimination concerning capabilities as a person ages; it's not just about absolute capacities, but what society idealizes in terms of its workers).

The expectation of a 30-40 year working life beginning at roughly 20 years old, with retirement at 60-65 means what we're doing is increasing the size of the population that isn't working, and constantly feeding a bubble of people who are not productive (rather, they are tax burdens) while the boundaries of what we consider the working age are static. This is not sustainable, but neither is it an easy problem to fix. You either reduce the size of that population, or you must find a way for older and older people to continue to feasibly earn an income by doing something effectively productive for society. Then again, another problem raised by this is: opportunity. Any category of work that we might find is suitable for the older class would steal opportunity from the younger generations, who themselves have been shifting for years toward more sedentary styles of work (the same work that the older generation would compete for; take data entry, or remote coding or billing services).

Taking a step further backward, our economies are not designed for this type of situation, that is, for life extension. Every economic theory - even if it doesn't say so explicitly - assumes a regular cycle of birth, life, and death. The old die at approximately the right time to pass on their inherited wealth and opportunity to the next generation. This is built in to the concept of economy itself. But we are now experiencing a generation of older, retired people that are not participating in this cycle. They are expecting longer lives, and they are also operating on a different value set/paradigm about the human life cycle, i.e. not that we live to eventually die for our progeny, but that we live for ourselves, and we live as long as possible to have as much as we can at the end. Rather than seeing a world with hope and opportunity to revivify the generations that are coming after them. We've lost the fundamental place that sacrifice played in the life of humanity. This is not all the fault of old people, however, because the young have also devalued the old. Old age is senility and irrelevance, as opposed to revered elder-ship. I think as a collective (and unconsciously) the aging folks have perceived their dismissal by the young, and this all has to do with the dissolution of our social glue of family structures and community. We broke the natural order and it's breaking us back.

An economy cannot fix this. The sacrifice has to be genuine. We could imagine a society where the sacrifice was programmed (in the systemic way that it is in Communism), and it doesn't work. Life could not be meaningful and there could be no striving if you knew that all of your energetic output and struggle would be taken from you for the faceless, foggy value of "the group".This was one of the underlying technological feats of Christ on human psychology.
